Warp-based methods were introduced as a class of space-time representations that condition the representation with a time component [S1].

The claim states that warp-based methods are a class of space-time representations that condition the representation with a time component. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly categorizes 'Warping-based Methods' under the broader context of space-time representations (Section 6.2 is titled 'Space-time Representations' and Section 6.1 'Warping-based Methods' is presented as a specific approach within this domain). The text describes how these methods model geometry and appearance as a continuous function of both space and time, and specifically mentions that they learn a deformation field to warp points to their state at 'each time step', thereby conditioning the representation on time. The mathematical formulation $f = F(T(p, C_0))$ and the discussion of forward/backward warps across time steps confirm that the representation is conditioned on the time component via the deformation/warping process.
supported
*   **Discontinuous Mapping:** Backward warps often result in discontinuous mappings because various object configurations can occupy the same spatial location at different time steps [S1].

The claim states that backward warps often result in discontinuous mappings because various object configurations can occupy the same spatial location at different time steps. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'when attempting to map 3D points back to the canonical space across different time steps, the backward warp often results in discontinuous mapping, as various object configurations can occupy the same spatial location.' This matches the claim exactly.

Warp-based dynamic scene representations model temporal changes by learning a temporally global 3D canonical representation and a learnable, time-dependent deformation field to warp canonical space to match observed scenes at each timestep [S1].

The claim states that warp-based dynamic scene representations model temporal changes by learning a temporally global 3D canonical representation and a learnable, time-dependent deformation field to warp canonical space to match observed scenes at each timestep. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 6.1: 'Warping-based methods... first learn a temporally global 3D representation, referred to as a canonical representation. The motion is then modeled by a deformation field, which can be used to warp all the 3D points in the canonical space to their deformed state at each time step.' This directly supports every part of the claim.

2.  **Learn Deformation Field:** Learn a deformation field $T$ that maps points between the canonical space and the deformed space at specific time steps [S1].

The claim states that the method involves learning a deformation field T that maps points between the canonical space and the deformed space at specific time steps. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 6.1, stating that 'The motion is then modeled by a deformation field, which can be used to warp all the 3D points in the canonical space to their deformed state at each time step.' It further defines T as a deformation network mapping a point p to its canonical counterpart p' (or vice versa depending on forward/backward warp context, but fundamentally mapping between canonical and deformed spaces) and notes that this is done at 'each time step' or 'dynamic time steps'. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
3.  **Render:** Query the static representation $F$ at the warped canonical point $p'$ to obtain the field value $\xi$ [S1].

The claim states that the static representation $F$ is queried at the warped canonical point $p'$ to obtain the field value $	ext{xi}$. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly defines the relationship as $f = F 	ext{ o } T$ with $T : (p, 	ext{C}_0) 	o p'$ and $F : p'[	ext{d}; 	ext{C}] 	o 	ext{xi}$. This confirms that $p'$ is the input to $F$ (the static representation) and $	ext{xi}$ is the output, which matches the claim exactly.

1.  **Learn Canonical Representation:** Learn a temporally global 3D representation (canonical space) that captures the static geometry and appearance of the scene [S1].

It further explains that this representation is static (inferred by function F from the canonical point p') and captures the scene's properties, while motion is handled by a deformation field. The claim accurately reflects the core definition provided in the evidence.

Unlike [Space-time representations](6885-space-time-representations.md), which extend the query space to include time directly, warp-based methods explicitly separate geometry and appearance into a static component and a deformation component [S1].

The evidence explicitly contrasts warp-based methods with space-time representations. It states that space-time representations 'extend the query space... to include time' (matching the claim's description of extending the query space to include time directly). Conversely, it describes warp-based methods as learning a 'temporally global 3D representation' (canonical/static component) and a 'deformation field' (deformation component) to warp points, thereby separating geometry/appearance into these two distinct parts. The claim accurately reflects the definitions and distinctions provided in the text.
